title: Inherited Metabolic & White Matter Disorders
summary: Genetic disorders of metabolism, myelin and motor neurons that injure the developing nervous system.

lessons.title: PKU and Newborn Screening for Brain Disorders

levels.kid:
Your body is like a busy kitchen. Food comes in, and tiny helpers called **enzymes** chop it into useful pieces.

Some babies are born missing one helper. In **PKU**, the missing helper should break down a piece of protein called **phenylalanine**. Without it, phenylalanine piles up in the blood, like dishes stacking up in a sink. Too much of it can hurt the growing brain.

Here is the good news. When babies are just a day or two old, a nurse takes a few drops of blood from the heel. Scientists test the drops. If a baby has PKU, the family starts a special diet very early. Then the brain can grow healthy and strong. A tiny test protects a whole life!
levels.hs:
**Phenylketonuria (PKU)** is an inherited disease where the body can't properly process **phenylalanine (Phe)**, an amino acid found in protein foods. The enzyme **phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH)** normally turns Phe into another amino acid, **tyrosine**, in the liver. In PKU, mutations in the *PAH* gene mean the enzyme doesn't work well, so Phe builds up to toxic levels in the blood and brain.

PKU is **autosomal recessive**: a child must inherit a faulty copy of the gene from both parents. Carrier parents are healthy. It affects roughly 1 in 10,000-15,000 babies of European ancestry.

Untreated, PKU causes severe intellectual disability, seizures, behavior problems, eczema, lighter skin and hair, and a musty body odor. Babies look normal at birth, so the damage happens silently.

That is why **newborn screening** exists. In the early 1960s, **Robert Guthrie** invented a test using dried blood spots on filter paper. Today a few drops from a baby's heel, collected in the first days of life, are tested for PKU and dozens of other conditions.

Treatment is a lifelong **low-phenylalanine diet** with a special protein formula. Babies treated early grow up with normal or near-normal intelligence. PKU is the classic example of a genetic brain disease where early detection changes everything.
levels.college:
**PKU biochemistry.** Phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), a liver enzyme, hydroxylates phenylalanine to tyrosine. It needs three partners:
- the cofactor **tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4)**
- molecular oxygen
- non-heme iron

When PAH is deficient, Phe accumulates. Excess Phe is shunted into minor pathways that make **phenylketones** such as phenylpyruvate, which gave the disease its name. Følling identified these compounds in patients' urine in 1934.

**Why the brain suffers.** Phe crosses the blood-brain barrier on the **LAT1** large neutral amino acid transporter. Other large neutral amino acids use the same carrier, including tyrosine and tryptophan. High Phe outcompetes them, which:
- lowers brain synthesis of dopamine and serotonin
- impairs protein synthesis
- disrupts **myelination**, leaving white matter changes on MRI

Tyrosine itself becomes conditionally essential.

**Genetics.** PKU is autosomal recessive. More than 1,000 *PAH* variants are known. Many patients are compound heterozygotes, and genotype loosely predicts severity. The spectrum runs from classic PKU to milder hyperphenylalaninemia.

**BH4 defects.** About 1-2% of hyperphenylalaninemia comes from defects in BH4 synthesis or recycling. BH4 is also the cofactor for tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylases, so these children lack neurotransmitters even when Phe is controlled. They must be distinguished from PAH deficiency by measuring urine/blood pterins and dihydropteridine reductase (DHPR) activity.

**Newborn screening.** Guthrie's bacterial inhibition assay used a *Bacillus subtilis* strain whose growth Phe overcame. Modern programs use **tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS)** on dried blood spots. It measures Phe and the **Phe/Tyr ratio**, plus many amino acids and acylcarnitines in one run. Screening follows the **Wilson-Jungner criteria**: the condition must be important, detectable before symptoms, and treatable.

**Maternal PKU.** High maternal Phe crosses the placenta and harms the fetus. It can cause microcephaly, intellectual disability and congenital heart defects. Good metabolic control before conception prevents this.
levels.phd:
**Molecular pathology of PAH.** PAH is a homotetramer, with each subunit made of a regulatory, a catalytic and a tetramerization domain. It shows positive cooperativity and is allosterically activated when Phe binds the regulatory domain. Most pathogenic variants are missense. They act mainly through **protein misfolding**, which accelerates degradation, rather than by abolishing the active site. That is why some mutant enzymes respond to excess BH4, which acts as a **pharmacological chaperone**: it stabilizes the protein and raises residual activity. **Sapropterin** (synthetic 6R-BH4) is approved on this basis. Responsiveness is tested by a loading trial. It is common in mild genotypes, such as those carrying R261Q or Y414C, and rare with null alleles like R408W, the most frequent European variant.

**Pathogenesis.** The leading model is competitive transport at the blood-brain barrier. LAT1 has a low Km for Phe relative to its plasma concentration, so modest Phe elevations sharply reduce brain influx of other large neutral amino acids. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy shows brain Phe roughly tracking plasma Phe, with individual variability in transport. This variability helps explain why some untreated adults are surprisingly spared. Proposed downstream mechanisms include:
- deficits in dopamine and serotonin
- inhibition of pyruvate kinase and HMG-CoA reductase, with cholesterol relevant to myelin
- oxidative stress
- amyloid-like Phe fibrils, a contested hypothesis

**Diet as a natural experiment.** Bickel's 1953 report of dietary Phe restriction in a child, followed by universal screening, created one of medicine's clearest gene-environment demonstrations. The genotype stays the same, yet the phenotype depends on the environment. PKU therefore became the textbook rebuttal to genetic determinism.

**Screening science.** Screening thresholds trade sensitivity against specificity. The Phe/Tyr ratio reduces false positives from prematurity, parenteral nutrition and early sampling. Early discharge was once worried to cause false negatives before Phe rises, but protein intake within the first 24-48 h is usually enough for MS/MS. The US **Recommended Uniform Screening Panel (RUSP)** now lists over 35 core conditions. Inclusion rests on formal evidence review of treatability and of analytic validity.

**Controversy.** Some argue for "diet for life" and others for relaxation in adulthood. Evidence of subtle executive dysfunction, mood symptoms and white matter changes with poor adult control has largely favored lifelong treatment.
levels.expert:
**Current management targets.** The 2014 ACMG guideline and the 2017 European guideline both recommend lifelong treatment. Their blood Phe targets differ somewhat with age, especially for adults, so it is worth checking which guideline a clinic follows. Adherence collapses in adolescence because the diet is restrictive, unpalatable and socially isolating. That makes adolescence the main real-world failure point, not the screening test.

**Therapies beyond diet.**
- **Sapropterin**: benefits only BH4-responsive patients, often allowing more natural protein.
- **Pegvaliase** (PEGylated *Anabaena variabilis* phenylalanine ammonia lyase, approved 2018 for adults): converts Phe to trans-cinnamic acid and ammonia, independent of PAH. It can achieve normal Phe on an unrestricted diet. Its key liability is immunogenicity, including anaphylaxis. Patients are prescribed auto-injectable epinephrine, and treatment requires an induction-titration period.
- **Sepiapterin**: a BH4 precursor with more efficient cellular uptake. It was approved in 2025 after phase 3 data showed Phe lowering across a broader range of genotypes than sapropterin.
- **Investigational**: AAV liver-directed *PAH* gene therapy, mRNA therapy, base editing of common variants such as R408W, engineered probiotic bacteria and LAT1 blockade with large neutral amino acid supplements. Durability in the growing liver, where hepatocyte turnover dilutes AAV episomes, remains a central problem for pediatric gene therapy.

**Diagnostic pitfalls.**
- Always exclude **BH4 disorders** in any positive screen. Missing GTP cyclohydrolase, PTPS or DHPR deficiency means missing a treatable neurotransmitter disease that diet alone won't fix.
- Transient hyperphenylalaninemia occurs in prematurity and liver immaturity.
- Specimens collected after transfusion can mislead screening.

**Maternal PKU** is now a major preventable cause of birth defects. Many women lost to follow-up after childhood are unaware of the risk. Strict Phe control before conception, continued through pregnancy, is the goal.

**Screening's frontier.** Genomic newborn screening pilots sequence hundreds of treatable-disease genes. Examples include GUARDIAN in New York, BabySeq and the UK Generation Study. They raise questions about variants of uncertain significance, late-onset conditions and consent. They also face a key limit: sequencing infers risk, whereas biochemistry measures actual metabolic state. Most experts envision genomics complementing, not replacing, MS/MS.

keyPoints: PKU is autosomal recessive PAH deficiency, so phenylalanine can't become tyrosine
Excess Phe floods LAT1 at the blood-brain barrier, starving the brain of other amino acids
Untreated PKU causes intellectual disability, seizures and white matter damage
Guthrie's heel-prick dried blood spot test began universal newborn screening; MS/MS is used today
Early low-Phe diet lets children develop normally; BH4 disorders must be excluded
Newer therapies: sapropterin, pegvaliase, sepiapterin, with gene therapy in trials

test.q: Which enzyme is deficient in classic PKU?
test.explain: PAH converts phenylalanine to tyrosine in the liver. Tyrosine hydroxylase acts later, making L-DOPA.

test.q: What is the inheritance pattern of PKU?
test.explain: A child needs two faulty PAH copies, one from each carrier parent.

test.q: Why does high blood phenylalanine harm the brain?
choices: It triggers an autoimmune attack on neurons
It outcompetes other amino acids for transport
It blocks oxygen binding to hemoglobin
test.explain: Phe competes on the LAT1 transporter, lowering brain tyrosine and tryptophan and so reducing neurotransmitter and protein synthesis.

test.q: Which modern method do most newborn screening labs use for PKU?
test.explain: MS/MS measures Phe and the Phe/Tyr ratio from dried blood spots, along with many other analytes. Guthrie's bacterial assay was the original method.

test.q: Why does a positive screen also need testing for BH4 defects?
choices: BH4 defects affect boys more often than girls
BH4 defects also impair neurotransmitter synthesis
BH4 defects are cured by a low-Phe diet alone
BH4 defects cause false positives in older infants
test.explain: BH4 is a cofactor for tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylases, so these children need neurotransmitter treatment beyond Phe control.

test.q: Which outcome is typical for a baby with PKU who starts the diet early?
choices: Severe intellectual disability by school age
test.explain: Early dietary treatment prevents the brain damage of untreated PKU.

test.q: What is the main risk of maternal PKU with poor control in pregnancy?
choices: The mother develops new liver failure
The placenta breaks down phenylalanine too fast
The baby inherits a dominant form of PKU
The fetus may have microcephaly and heart defects
test.explain: High maternal Phe crosses the placenta and harms fetal development, even in babies without PKU.

test.q: Which criteria are classically used to decide if a disease suits screening?
test.explain: Wilson-Jungner criteria ask whether a condition is important, detectable before symptoms and treatable.

test.q: Pegvaliase lowers phenylalanine by:
choices: Blocking Phe uptake in the gut
Converting Phe via an ammonia lyase
Restoring the patient's own PAH gene
Acting as a chaperone for misfolded PAH
test.explain: Pegvaliase is a bacterial phenylalanine ammonia lyase that turns Phe into trans-cinnamic acid, independent of PAH. Sapropterin is the chaperone.

test.q: Which scientist invented the dried blood spot test for PKU in the early 1960s?
test.explain: Robert Guthrie's filter-paper test launched universal newborn screening.

test.q: PAH normally converts phenylalanine into the amino acid ___.
test.explain: Tyrosine becomes conditionally essential in PKU.

test.q: The cofactor PAH needs is abbreviated ___.
test.explain: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) is also the cofactor for tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylases.

kidTest.q: What do enzymes do in your body?
kidTest.explain: Enzymes are tiny helpers that chop things up and change them.

kidTest.q: What piles up in the blood in PKU?
kidTest.explain: Phenylalanine is a piece of protein that can't be broken down in PKU.

kidTest.q: Where does the nurse take blood drops for the baby test?
kidTest.explain: A few drops come from the baby's heel.

kidTest.q: What helps a baby with PKU grow up healthy?
choices: Lots of extra sleep at night
kidTest.explain: Starting the special diet early protects the brain.

kidTest.q: PKU can hurt the growing b _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Too much phenylalanine can harm the brain, which is why early testing matters.

advancedTest.q: Why are mild PAH genotypes more often sapropterin-responsive than null alleles like R408W?
choices: Misfolded but present enzyme can be stabilized by excess cofactor acting as a chaperone
Mild variants are expressed in brain, where sapropterin acts directly
Null alleles raise liver BH4 synthesis, so added cofactor is redundant
Mild variants lack the regulatory domain, so added BH4 can reach the active site more easily
advancedTest.explain: Most missense variants destabilize PAH. Excess BH4 stabilizes residual protein, whereas null alleles leave nothing to rescue.

advancedTest.q: Some untreated adults with high plasma Phe have surprisingly mild cognitive effects. Which explanation best fits the lesson?
choices: Their kidneys excrete phenylketones fast enough to normalize plasma Phe
Individual variation in blood-brain barrier transport limits brain Phe
They carry heterozygous variants that are fully protective
Their tyrosine hydroxylase compensates by converting Phe to dopamine
advancedTest.explain: MRS shows that brain Phe varies between people at similar plasma levels, which is consistent with LAT1 transport variability.

advancedTest.q: Why is the Phe/Tyr ratio preferred over Phe alone in screening?
choices: It lets screening be done before any protein feeding
It reduces false positives from prematurity or parenteral nutrition
Tyrosine directly measures PAH gene copy number in blood
Tyrosine falls mainly in BH4 defects, so the ratio identifies them
advancedTest.explain: Phe can rise nonspecifically. Low tyrosine plus high Phe points to blocked conversion, improving specificity.

advancedTest.q: What is a central limitation of genomic newborn screening relative to MS/MS for PKU?
choices: Sequencing infers risk, while biochemistry measures actual metabolic state
Sequencing misses most missense variants in metabolic enzyme genes like PAH
Genomic screening requires samples taken after the first year
MS/MS detects variants of uncertain significance more often
advancedTest.explain: Variants of uncertain significance and penetrance make genotype an indirect signal, whereas MS/MS directly measures elevated Phe.

lessons.title: Lysosomal Storage Diseases: Tay-Sachs and Batten Disease

levels.kid:
Every cell in your body has tiny recycling bins called **lysosomes**. Inside them, special helpers called **enzymes** chop up old cell parts so they can be used again.

Sometimes a baby is born with a gene that has a mistake, so one enzyme is missing. Then the trash piles up instead of getting recycled. Brain cells are very sensitive to this, because most of them have to last a whole lifetime and cannot be replaced.

In **Tay-Sachs disease**, a fatty material builds up in brain cells. In **Batten disease**, a sticky material builds up. Over time the brain cells get sick. Children can slowly lose skills, like seeing or walking.

Scientists are working hard on new treatments, like replacing the missing enzyme.
levels.hs:
**Lysosomes** are acidic compartments inside cells, filled with about 60 **hydrolases**, enzymes that break down large molecules like fats, sugars and proteins. A **lysosomal storage disease (LSD)** happens when a gene variant disables one of these enzymes or a helper protein. The undigested material, called **storage material**, accumulates and damages the cell. There are over 70 LSDs. Together they affect roughly 1 in 5,000 births.

Neurons are especially vulnerable because they are **post-mitotic**: they don't divide, so they can't dilute the buildup. Most LSDs are **autosomal recessive**. A child must inherit two faulty copies, one from each carrier parent. Two carrier parents have a 25% chance with each pregnancy of having an affected child.

**Tay-Sachs disease** is caused by variants in **HEXA**, which encodes part of the enzyme **beta-hexosaminidase A**. Without it, a fatty molecule called **GM2 ganglioside** builds up in neurons. Babies seem normal at first. Around 3-6 months they show weakness, an exaggerated startle to sound, and later seizures and blindness. A classic sign is a **cherry-red spot** on the retina. The infantile form is usually fatal in early childhood.

**Batten disease** is the common name for the **neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (NCLs)**, a group caused by at least 13 genes (CLN1-CLN14). Many NCL forms begin with vision loss, then seizures and loss of skills.

Carrier screening in Ashkenazi Jewish communities, started in the 1970s, cut Tay-Sachs births there by over 90%.
levels.college:
Lysosomes degrade macromolecules at a pH of about 4.5-5. Soluble hydrolases are tagged with **mannose-6-phosphate (M6P)** in the Golgi and delivered by M6P receptors. Most LSDs result from loss of a single hydrolase, its activator, a membrane transporter, or this trafficking system.

**Tay-Sachs (GM2 gangliosidosis, B variant)**
- Hexosaminidase A is a heterodimer of an alpha subunit (HEXA, chromosome 15) and a beta subunit (HEXB).
- To cleave the terminal N-acetylgalactosamine from GM2 ganglioside, Hex A needs the **GM2 activator protein** (GM2A), which presents the lipid to the enzyme.
- Related disorders: HEXB loss causes **Sandhoff disease** (both Hex A and Hex B are lost). GM2A loss causes the AB variant.
- GM2 accumulates in neuronal lysosomes as **membranous cytoplasmic bodies** (onion-skin whorls on electron microscopy). Neurons swell, and the macula shows a cherry-red spot. Ganglion cells surround the fovea, which lacks them and stays red.
- Residual enzyme activity sets severity: infantile (near-zero activity), juvenile, and late-onset forms. Late-onset forms often show lower motor neuron and cerebellar signs in adults.

**Batten disease (NCLs)**
- The common feature is autofluorescent **lipopigment** storage.
- **CLN1/PPT1** (palmitoyl-protein thioesterase 1) causes the infantile form. Storage appears as **granular osmiophilic deposits**.
- **CLN2/TPP1** (tripeptidyl peptidase 1) causes the late-infantile form. Onset is around 2-4 years, often with seizures and language delay. Storage appears as curvilinear profiles.
- **CLN3** encodes a lysosomal membrane protein and causes the classic juvenile form. Vision loss begins around age 4-7, followed by cognitive decline and seizures. Storage appears as fingerprint profiles.
- In CLN2 and CLN3, the main stored protein is **subunit c of mitochondrial ATP synthase**. In CLN1, it is the saposins.

Diagnosis combines enzyme assays (Hex A, PPT1, TPP1 in blood or fibroblasts), genetic testing, and eye exams. **Cerliponase alfa**, a recombinant TPP1 delivered into the brain's ventricles, is the first approved therapy for CLN2 (FDA, 2017).
levels.phd:
LSD pathology extends well beyond 'full bins.' Storage triggers secondary cascades:
- impaired autophagic flux and buildup of autophagosomes
- lysosomal membrane permeabilization
- disrupted calcium homeostasis and endoplasmic reticulum stress
- defective mitochondrial turnover
- microglial and astrocytic activation

These downstream effects explain why the amount of storage correlates imperfectly with neuronal death. In Sandhoff (Hexb-/-) mice, neurodegeneration is preceded by microglial activation and macrophage infiltration. Removing MIP-1alpha (CCL3) delays disease, which implicates inflammation as a driver of damage.

**The Hex A threshold.** Conzelmann and Sandhoff proposed a critical-threshold model. Disease appears only when Hex A activity falls below roughly 10-15% of normal, because GM2 degradation depends nonlinearly on enzyme and activator. This explains why carriers, with about 50% activity, are healthy. It also explains why small amounts of residual activity in late-onset patients delay symptoms by decades.

**A mouse paradox.** Hexa-/- mice are nearly asymptomatic. Mice can bypass the block through a sialidase (Neu3) that converts GM2 to GA2, which Hex B can degrade. Hexa/Neu3 double knockouts recapitulate the disease. This species difference complicated early modeling.

**Population genetics.** Carrier frequency is about 1 in 27-30 in Ashkenazi Jews, compared with about 1 in 250-300 generally. The common alleles are a 4-bp insertion in exon 11 and an intron 12 splice variant, plus G269S in late-onset disease. Founder effect and drift are favored over heterozygote advantage. Elevated frequencies also occur in French Canadians, Cajuns, and Old Order Amish.

**NCL biology.** Many NCL proteins are not hydrolases at all. CLN3, CLN7/MFSD8, and CLN8 are membrane proteins, and CLN5 has been proposed as a bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate (BMP) synthase (2023). BMP is an internal lysosomal lipid required for lipid degradation. That NCLs store protein (subunit c, saposins) rather than a substrate predicted by the enzyme defect remains mechanistically puzzling. Loss of CLN3 alters glycerophosphodiester handling, suggesting a lysosomal phospholipid-recycling role. Variants in the same genes can cause adult-onset or nonsyndromic retinal disease, so the NCLs form a spectrum rather than discrete diseases.
levels.expert:
Therapeutic strategies for neuronopathic LSDs are shaped by the **blood-brain barrier**. Intravenous enzyme replacement, effective for visceral Gaucher type 1 or Fabry disease, does not reach neurons. This is why cerliponase alfa is given intracerebroventricularly every two weeks through an implanted reservoir.

In the pivotal trial, treated CLN2 children showed markedly slower decline in motor-language scores than natural-history controls. Treatment does not halt retinal degeneration, so intravitreal approaches are being explored. Reservoir infections and device failures are real burdens.

**Gene therapy.** For GM2 gangliosidoses, AAV approaches must restore both subunits in the correct ratio. Bicistronic constructs (HEXA plus HEXB) delivered intrathecally or intraparenchymally have entered early human studies. In parallel, engineered variants that still use GM2A (the hybrid 'HexM' enzyme forming a stable homodimer) have been developed. The Tay-Sachs/Sandhoff field has also benefited from naturally occurring disease in cats and sheep, whose larger brains test vector distribution better than mice.

**Substrate reduction therapy.** This approach inhibits glucosylceramide synthase to lower glycosphingolipid production. Miglustat failed to change outcomes in late-onset GM2. Brain-penetrant agents such as venglustat were tested, with disappointing GM2 results, which highlights the difficulty of lowering flux enough. N-acetyl-L-leucine has shown symptomatic benefit in GM2 trials.

**Antisense and individualized therapy.** Milasen, a splice-correcting antisense oligonucleotide designed for a single child with CLN7 Batten disease (Kim et al., NEJM 2019), became a landmark for 'n-of-1' therapeutics. It raised regulatory and ethical questions about evidence standards, cost, and equity.

**Clinical pitfalls.**
- Late-onset Tay-Sachs is often misdiagnosed as ALS, spinal muscular atrophy, or psychiatric illness. Psychosis occurs in a subset of patients.
- Enzyme assays can be confounded by pseudodeficiency alleles that lower activity against artificial substrates but not natural ones. Confirm with genotyping.
- A juvenile NCL often presents first to ophthalmology as unexplained retinal dystrophy. Vacuolated lymphocytes on a blood smear are a cheap clue to CLN3.
- Expanded carrier screening panels now include HEXA regardless of ancestry, because enzyme-based screening misses some carriers and ancestry-based targeting is imprecise.

**Open questions.** Why do neurons die when storage alone correlates poorly with loss? What is the therapeutic window before irreversible damage? Can pre-symptomatic treatment, via newborn screening, achieve what treating symptomatic children cannot?

keyPoints: Lysosomes use enzymes to recycle large molecules; a missing enzyme causes storage disease
Neurons are vulnerable because they don't divide and can't dilute buildup
Tay-Sachs: HEXA variants, hexosaminidase A loss, GM2 ganglioside storage, cherry-red spot
Batten disease = neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (CLN genes), often starting with vision loss
Most LSDs are autosomal recessive; carrier screening cut Tay-Sachs births sharply
Cerliponase alfa, given into the brain's ventricles, treats CLN2 because enzymes don't cross the blood-brain barrier

test.q: What directly causes a lysosomal storage disease?
choices: Loss of function of a lysosomal protein
Infection of lysosomes by a virus
Excess production of a lysosomal enzyme
test.explain: Loss of a hydrolase, activator, transporter or trafficking protein prevents breakdown, so material accumulates.

test.q: Which gene is mutated in Tay-Sachs disease?
test.explain: HEXA encodes the alpha subunit of hexosaminidase A. HEXB loss causes Sandhoff disease instead.

test.q: Which molecule accumulates in Tay-Sachs neurons?
test.explain: Without hexosaminidase A, GM2 ganglioside cannot be broken down and builds up in neuronal lysosomes.

test.q: Why does Tay-Sachs produce a cherry-red spot on the macula?
choices: The optic nerve swells from raised brain pressure
Blood vessels grow abnormally in the fovea
Swollen ganglion cells surround a fovea that lacks them
Pigment from storage material stains the retina red
test.explain: Lipid-laden ganglion cells turn the retina pale, while the fovea, which lacks ganglion cells, stays red.

test.q: Two carrier parents for Tay-Sachs have what chance per pregnancy of an affected child?
test.explain: In autosomal recessive inheritance, each child has a 1 in 4 chance of inheriting two faulty copies.

test.q: Why are neurons especially vulnerable to storage diseases?
choices: They divide too quickly to clear waste
They are post-mitotic and can't dilute buildup
They rely on glycogen for their energy
They contain very few lysosomes to clear waste
test.explain: Neurons don't divide, so stored material accumulates over a lifetime instead of being diluted.

test.q: Batten disease is the common name for which group of disorders?
test.explain: Batten disease refers to the NCLs, caused by CLN genes and marked by autofluorescent lipopigment storage.

test.q: A child with classic juvenile CLN3 disease most often first shows:
test.explain: Juvenile CLN3 typically begins with vision loss around age 4-7, before cognitive decline and seizures.

test.q: Why is cerliponase alfa delivered into the brain's ventricles?
choices: Enzyme given by vein can't reach neurons
It is broken down quickly by stomach acid
It acts mainly on spinal cord motor neurons
It is designed to act mainly on the retina
test.explain: Large recombinant enzymes given by vein do not cross the blood-brain barrier to reach neurons, so the drug is infused intracerebroventricularly.

test.q: Soluble lysosomal enzymes are targeted to lysosomes by a mannose-6-___ tag.
test.explain: The M6P tag added in the Golgi is recognized by M6P receptors that deliver enzymes to lysosomes.

test.q: Which CLN gene's enzyme (TPP1) is replaced by cerliponase alfa?
test.explain: CLN2 encodes tripeptidyl peptidase 1. Its deficiency causes late-infantile Batten disease.

test.q: Lysosomal enzymes that break down molecules using water are called ___.
test.explain: Lysosomes hold about 60 hydrolases that work best at acidic pH.

kidTest.q: What do lysosomes do in a cell?
kidTest.explain: Lysosomes are the cell's recycling bins.

kidTest.q: What happens when an enzyme is missing?
choices: The cell turns a new color
Trash piles up in the cell
kidTest.explain: Without the enzyme, material can't be chopped up, so it builds up.

kidTest.q: Why are brain cells easily hurt by this buildup?
choices: They have to last a whole lifetime
They are very tiny and soft
kidTest.explain: Most brain cells can't be replaced, so the buildup keeps growing.

kidTest.q: What kind of material builds up in Tay-Sachs disease?
kidTest.explain: In Tay-Sachs, a fatty material piles up in brain cells.

kidTest.q: The helpers that chop up old cell parts are called e _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Enzymes are the helpers that break things down in lysosomes.

advancedTest.q: Tay-Sachs carriers have about 50% Hex A activity yet are healthy. The best explanation is:
choices: Heterozygous neurons store GM2 in glia rather than in lysosomes
Disease requires activity below a critical threshold of roughly 10-15%
Hex B fully compensates for the missing alpha subunit in human neurons
Carriers produce extra GM2 activator protein that removes the substrate
advancedTest.explain: The threshold model holds that GM2 breakdown stays adequate until activity drops below about 10-15%, so half activity is sufficient.

advancedTest.q: Why did Hexa-knockout mice fail to model Tay-Sachs until Neu3 was also deleted?
choices: Mouse microglia clear the excess GM2 before neurons are harmed
The mouse blood-brain barrier exports GM2 into the circulation
A mouse sialidase converts GM2 to GA2, which Hex B degrades
Mouse neurons lack GM2 ganglioside in their cell membranes
advancedTest.explain: The Neu3 bypass lets mice route GM2 through GA2 to Hex B. Removing it restores the human-like disease.

advancedTest.q: A low Hex A result on a screening assay in a healthy adult should prompt genotyping mainly because of:
choices: Carrier status being undetectable by any form of enzyme testing
Frequent false positives caused by elevated Hex B in older adults
Lab error from mannose-6-phosphate degradation in the blood sample
Pseudodeficiency alleles that lower activity on artificial substrates
advancedTest.explain: Pseudodeficiency alleles reduce activity in vitro but not against natural GM2, so genotyping prevents misclassification.

advancedTest.q: Which observation most challenges a simple 'storage equals toxicity' model in LSDs?
choices: Blocking inflammation in Sandhoff mice delays neurodegeneration
Most LSDs follow autosomal recessive inheritance
Enzyme replacement reduces storage in visceral organs
Storage material accumulates in lysosomes of affected neurons
advancedTest.explain: If removing CCL3 delays disease without removing storage, secondary inflammation drives damage, not storage alone.

lessons.title: Leukodystrophies: X-ALD, Krabbe and MLD

levels.kid:
Your brain sends messages along long, thin wires called nerves. Many of these wires wear a fatty coat called **myelin**, like the plastic coat on a phone charger cable. The coat helps messages zoom along fast.

Some children are born with a tiny spelling mistake in one gene. Because of it, their bodies cannot clean up or build myelin properly. The coat slowly breaks down. These illnesses are called **leukodystrophies**. "Leuko" means white, because myelin makes parts of the brain look white.

When the coat is damaged, messages slow down. Walking, talking and seeing can get harder.

Doctors can sometimes help a lot by giving new healthy blood-making cells or fixing the gene. These treatments work best when they start early, before the coat is badly hurt.
levels.hs:
**Leukodystrophies** are inherited diseases that damage the brain's **white matter**, the bundles of nerve fibers wrapped in **myelin**. Myelin is a fatty insulating layer made by cells called **oligodendrocytes**. It lets signals jump quickly along axons. When myelin is lost (**demyelination**) or never forms properly, nerve signals slow or fail.

Three classic examples:
- **X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD)**: a mutation in the **ABCD1** gene on the X chromosome. Very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs) build up in the brain and the adrenal glands. It mostly affects boys. The film *Lorenzo's Oil* told the story of one family.
- **Krabbe disease**: caused by missing the enzyme **galactocerebrosidase (GALC)**. A toxic lipid called psychosine kills myelin-making cells. Babies usually become very irritable and stiff in their first months.
- **Metachromatic leukodystrophy (MLD)**: caused by missing **arylsulfatase A (ARSA)**. Fats called sulfatides pile up inside lysosomes.

Krabbe and MLD are **autosomal recessive**, so a child needs two broken copies, one from each parent. X-ALD is **X-linked**. Boys have only one X, so one mutation is enough.

Doctors see the damage on **MRI** scans. Treatment with a **stem cell transplant** or **gene therapy** can slow or stop the disease. It works only if given before symptoms become severe. That is why X-ALD and Krabbe have been added to newborn screening in many places.
levels.college:
Leukodystrophies are genetic disorders that primarily affect CNS white matter. They may target myelin itself, oligodendrocytes, astrocytes or axons. Three prototypes illustrate peroxisomal and lysosomal mechanisms.

**X-ALD (ABCD1, Xq28)**
- ABCD1 encodes ALDP, a peroxisomal membrane transporter that imports very long-chain acyl-CoAs (e.g., C26:0) for **beta-oxidation**.
- Loss of ALDP raises plasma VLCFA. This elevated level is the diagnostic biomarker.
- Phenotypes are strikingly variable, even within one family:
  - **Childhood cerebral ALD**: inflammatory demyelination, typically at ages 4-10. It usually starts in the parieto-occipital white matter.
  - **Adrenomyeloneuropathy (AMN)**: a slowly progressive myelopathy in adults.
  - **Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)**: this can occur on its own.

**Krabbe disease (GALC, 14q31)**
- Galactocerebrosidase normally degrades galactosylceramide and **psychosine** (galactosylsphingosine).
- Psychosine is cytotoxic to oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells. This is the "psychosine hypothesis."
- The infantile form shows irritability, spasticity, feeding problems and peripheral neuropathy. Biopsy reveals **globoid cells**, which are multinucleated macrophages.

**MLD (ARSA, 22q13)**
- Arylsulfatase A deficiency causes sulfatide to accumulate in lysosomes.
- Under acidic cresyl violet stain, the stored material shows **metachromasia** (a color shift), which gives the disease its name.
- Forms are late-infantile, juvenile and adult. The adult form can begin with psychiatric or cognitive symptoms.
- MLD affects both central and peripheral myelin.

**Diagnosis**: MRI shows the white-matter pattern. Biochemistry (VLCFA levels, enzyme activity, psychosine) confirms it, followed by gene sequencing.

**Therapy**: Allogeneic **hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT)** lets donor-derived microglia-like cells repopulate the brain. HSCT and gene therapy help only when given early. In X-ALD this is judged by the **Loes score**, a 0-34 MRI severity scale.
levels.phd:
Mechanistically, these three disorders differ more than their shared radiology implies.

**X-ALD.** Accumulation of C26:0 in ALDP deficiency is necessary but not sufficient for cerebral disease. There is no genotype-phenotype correlation across more than 900 ABCD1 variants. Identical mutations yield cerebral ALD, AMN or no neurological disease within one kindred. This implicates modifiers: genetic, epigenetic and environmental factors (for example, head trauma has been reported as a trigger). The cerebral lesion is inflammatory. Microglial loss at the leading edge precedes demyelination. A gadolinium-enhancing rim marks blood-brain barrier breakdown and predicts progression. VLCFA incorporation into complex lipids (lysophosphatidylcholine C26:0, used in newborn screening) may drive oxidative stress and inflammasome activation. ABCD2 (ALDRP) partially overlaps in function, which motivates induction strategies. *Lorenzo's oil* (glyceryl trioleate/trierucate) lowers plasma VLCFA by competing for the ELOVL1 elongation pathway. Yet it does not reliably alter cerebral progression in symptomatic patients, which is a classic dissociation between biomarker and outcome.

**Krabbe.** Suzuki and Miyatake's 1972 **psychosine hypothesis** remains central. Galactosylceramide itself is stored inside macrophages to form globoid cells. In contrast, psychosine is toxic at low concentrations. It disrupts lipid rafts and PKC signaling and inhibits cytochrome c oxidase. More recent work shows that psychosine arises largely by acid ceramidase deacylation of galactosylceramide, not by a separate synthesis pathway. Genetic or pharmacologic ablation of acid ceramidase rescues the twitcher mouse (a naturally occurring Galc mutant). The common European 30-kb deletion allele causes the severe infantile form.

**MLD.** Residual ARSA activity correlates with onset: null alleles produce late-infantile disease. A major pitfall is **ARSA pseudodeficiency**. Common polymorphisms (e.g., c.1049A>G) lower measured activity in roughly 1-2% of people without causing disease. Diagnosis therefore requires urinary sulfatide measurement or genetic confirmation. Saposin B deficiency (PSAP) mimics MLD despite normal ARSA activity.

HSCT benefit depends on how slowly donor myeloid cells engraft the brain, which takes months. This is a kinetic problem that rapidly progressive infantile disease often outruns.
levels.expert:
Clinical practice in leukodystrophies is now shaped by approved gene therapies and expanding newborn screening.

**Approved lentiviral therapies.** Autologous HSC gene therapy uses the patient's own cells. Because there is no allogeneic donor, it avoids graft-versus-host disease.
- **Atidarsagene autotemcel (Libmeldy/Lenmeldy)**, for MLD, was approved in the EU in 2020 and by the FDA in 2024. It is indicated for presymptomatic late-infantile and early-juvenile disease, and for early-symptomatic early-juvenile disease. Supraphysiological ARSA expression from engineered cells cross-corrects neighboring cells, outperforming allogeneic HSCT.
- **Elivaldogene autotemcel (Skysona)**, for early cerebral ALD, received accelerated FDA approval in 2022. Its label now carries a boxed warning: hematologic malignancies, including myelodysplastic syndrome, have been linked to insertional activation near oncogenes such as MECOM. This shifts the risk-benefit calculation relative to allogeneic HSCT when a matched donor exists. The FDA later restricted its use to patients without an available HLA-matched donor.

**Screening dilemmas.**
- X-ALD was added to the US Recommended Uniform Screening Panel (RUSP) in 2016. Screened boys need serial MRI (roughly every 6-12 months in early childhood) and adrenal testing, since adrenal insufficiency is a treatable, life-threatening finding.
- Screening also detects heterozygous girls, many of whom develop myelopathy in midlife. This upends the old idea that carriers are "asymptomatic." It also finds Zellweger-spectrum disorders and boys who may never develop cerebral disease, so families face years of uncertainty.
- Krabbe joined the RUSP in 2024. Low GALC activity alone overcalls disease, so psychosine serves as a second-tier test to stratify risk.

**Timing.** In infantile Krabbe, HSCT in the first weeks of life changes the natural history. It still leaves progressive peripheral neuropathy and motor decline, showing that systemic myeloid correction poorly reaches Schwann cells.

**Open questions.**
- What triggers the conversion to cerebral ALD? Candidate modifiers and plasma biomarkers such as neurofilament light are being studied.
- Can CNS-targeted AAV approaches outpace the slow engraftment of myeloid cells?
- Is leriglitazone, a PPAR-gamma agonist that has been trialed in AMN and cerebral ALD, of real benefit?
- How should gene therapy be offered to symptomatic patients?

For neurosurgery, intracerebral and intrathecal delivery routes for enzyme and vector are an active translational frontier.

keyPoints: Leukodystrophies are genetic diseases of CNS white matter and myelin
X-ALD: ABCD1 mutation, peroxisomal VLCFA buildup, X-linked
Krabbe: GALC deficiency; toxic psychosine kills oligodendrocytes
MLD: ARSA deficiency; sulfatide storage, metachromatic staining
HSCT and gene therapy work only before advanced symptoms
Newborn screening enables presymptomatic treatment

Varying VLCFA levels that fully set the phenotype
Different ABCD1 alleles inherited by each brother
Modifier factors beyond the ABCD1 genotype

choices: It induces ABCD2 to compensate for the deficiency
It blocks the main route that forms psychosine
It increases galactosylceramide clearance in macrophages
It restores GALC enzyme expression in neurons

Allogeneic cells engraft in the brain far faster

Allogeneic HSCT has no graft-versus-host risk

lessons.title: Mitochondrial Disease and Leigh Syndrome

levels.kid:
Inside almost every cell in your body are tiny power plants called **mitochondria**. They turn food and oxygen into energy the cell can use.

The brain is a very hungry organ. It uses lots of energy all day and all night. So when the power plants don't work well, the brain and muscles feel it first.

Mitochondria are special because they carry a few of their own genes. You get those genes only from your mom.

In a disease called **Leigh syndrome**, the power plants break down in young children. Parts of the brain that control moving, breathing and swallowing get hurt. Doctors look for clues with brain pictures and blood tests. Scientists are working hard on new ways to help.
levels.hs:
**Mitochondria** are organelles that make most of a cell's energy molecule, **ATP**, through a process called **oxidative phosphorylation** (OXPHOS). Oxygen is the final acceptor of electrons passed along a chain of protein complexes.

Mitochondrial disease happens when this energy system fails. It can come from two genomes:
- **Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA)**: a small circle of 16,569 base pairs with 37 genes. It is inherited only from the mother.
- **Nuclear DNA**: over 1,000 nuclear genes make mitochondrial proteins. These follow normal patterns like autosomal recessive.

A cell holds hundreds to thousands of mtDNA copies. If only some carry a mutation, this mix is called **heteroplasmy**. Symptoms usually appear once the mutant fraction passes a **threshold**.

The brain, muscles, heart and eyes need the most energy, so they suffer most. When OXPHOS fails, cells switch to making energy without oxygen, producing **lactate**. High lactate in blood or spinal fluid is a classic clue.

The most common mitochondrial disease of infancy is **Leigh syndrome** (subacute necrotizing encephalomyelopathy). Children, often under 2, lose skills they had learned, especially after an infection. They develop weak muscle tone, trouble swallowing, abnormal eye movements and breathing problems. MRI shows symmetric damage in the **basal ganglia** and **brainstem**. Over 100 different genes can cause it.
levels.college:
**Leigh syndrome (LS)** is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by defective mitochondrial energy production. Its incidence is roughly 1 in 40,000 births. It is the archetype of **genetic heterogeneity**: more than 110 genes in both genomes are implicated.

**The OXPHOS machinery**
- Complexes I-IV form the electron transport chain; complex V (ATP synthase) uses the proton gradient to make ATP.
- mtDNA encodes 13 OXPHOS subunits, 22 tRNAs and 2 rRNAs. The rest of the roughly 90 OXPHOS subunits, and all assembly factors, are nuclear-encoded.
- The **pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDHc)** links glycolysis to the citric acid cycle. PDHc deficiency, often from X-linked **PDHA1**, also causes LS.

**Common causes**
- **Complex I** deficiency is the most frequent biochemical defect, with nuclear genes like NDUFS4 and mtDNA genes like MT-ND5.
- **SURF1**, a complex IV assembly factor, is a classic autosomal recessive cause.
- **MT-ATP6** m.8993T>G: at high heteroplasmy (above about 90%) it causes maternally inherited LS. At lower levels the same variant causes **NARP** (neuropathy, ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa).

**Why these lesions?** The basal ganglia, thalamus and brainstem have very high metabolic demand and limited reserve. Crises triggered by fever or fasting push them past the threshold, producing spongiform necrosis, demyelination, gliosis and capillary proliferation.

**Diagnosis**
- Elevated **lactate** in blood and especially CSF; a lactate peak on **MR spectroscopy**.
- Symmetric T2 hyperintensities in the putamen, globus pallidus and brainstem.
- Genetic testing (exome or genome sequencing plus mtDNA sequencing) has largely replaced muscle biopsy as the first test.

Related mtDNA syndromes include **MELAS** (m.3243A>G in MT-TL1, with stroke-like episodes) and **MERRF** (m.8344A>G, with myoclonic epilepsy).
levels.phd:
Mitochondrial genetics breaks Mendelian rules in several ways. Because mtDNA is polyploid, the phenotype depends on the **heteroplasmy level**, which can differ between tissues and drift over time.

The **mitochondrial genetic bottleneck** explains why heteroplasmy can shift sharply in one generation. In the female germline, a reduced effective number of segregating mtDNA units means offspring can inherit very different mutant loads from the same mother. Classic cow and mouse studies, and later human oocyte data, support random genetic drift, though selection against severe variants also acts in the germline. Mitotic segregation in dividing tissues, and relaxed replication in postmitotic neurons, further spread out heteroplasmy between tissues. Blood levels of m.3243A>G fall with age, so urine epithelium is a better sample.

Threshold effects are biochemical: mutant mitochondrial tRNAs (MELAS, MERRF) impair translation of all 13 mtDNA-encoded subunits. These variants often need about 80-90% load for clinical expression, while some protein-coding variants act at lower loads.

Leigh syndrome's lesion pattern reflects more than ATP supply. Ndufs4 knockout mice show that loss of complex I subunit NDUFS4 only in glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons (notably in the vestibular nuclei and olfactory bulb) reproduces the fatal phenotype. Their microglial activation and the striking rescue by **chronic hypoxia** (Jain et al., 2016) suggest that **oxygen toxicity**, not just energy failure, drives neurodegeneration: unused oxygen accumulates in tissue when the chain cannot consume it. Rapamycin (mTOR inhibition) also extended survival (Johnson et al., 2013), linking nutrient signaling to disease.

Diagnostic yield has changed: functional OXPHOS assays from muscle can miss tissue-specific defects, while genome sequencing now achieves molecular diagnosis in a majority of LS cases. Multi-omic approaches (RNA-seq for splicing, proteomics for complex assembly) resolve many variants of uncertain significance.

Controversy persists about whether "Leigh-like" cases with atypical imaging belong to the same entity. Biochemical complex deficiency also correlates imperfectly with genotype, because assembly factors cause multiple complex defects.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the priority in suspected Leigh syndrome is to find **treatable mimics and treatable causes** before settling on supportive care.

Do not miss:
- **Biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease** (SLC19A3): imaging resembles LS, and it responds dramatically to biotin and thiamine. Early recognition prevents permanent injury.
- **Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency** (e.g., COQ2, PDSS2): may respond to CoQ10 supplementation.
- **PDHc deficiency**: the ketogenic diet bypasses the block by supplying acetyl-CoA from fat, and some PDHA1 variants are thiamine-responsive.
- **ECHS1 and HIBCH** defects (valine catabolism): toxic intermediates. Valine restriction is under study.

Acute management pitfalls:
- **Valproate** is contraindicated in POLG disease because of liver failure risk. Caution also applies to other mitochondrial disorders.
- Avoid prolonged fasting. Treat fever and infection aggressively, since crises cause stepwise regression.
- Anesthesia needs planning: prolonged propofol infusion and lactate-containing fluids warrant caution.
- Central respiratory failure from brainstem lesions is the main cause of death. Families should discuss goals of care early.

Advances:
- **Mitochondrial donation** (pronuclear transfer) to prevent mtDNA disease transmission is licensed in the UK; births were reported in 2025. Low-level carryover of maternal mtDNA, with occasional reversion, remains a concern.
- **Preimplantation genetic testing** selects embryos with low heteroplasmy for some variants.
- **Gene therapy**: AAV-mediated NDUFS4 replacement rescues mouse models. Mitochondrially targeted base editors (DdCBEs, derived from the bacterial toxin DddA) can edit mtDNA directly, which was impossible with CRISPR because guide RNAs are not imported.
- **Heteroplasmy shifting** with mitochondrially targeted nucleases (mitoTALENs, mitoZFNs) selectively destroys mutant genomes.
- Drug trials (e.g., the redox modulator vatiquinone/EPI-743) have mostly missed primary endpoints. This reflects small cohorts, heterogeneous genotypes and a lack of validated outcome measures.

Open questions include why particular nuclei are vulnerable, whether hypoxia-mimicking strategies can be translated safely, and how to design trials for ultra-rare genotypes.

keyPoints: Mitochondria make ATP by oxidative phosphorylation (complexes I-V)
mtDNA is maternally inherited; most mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded
Heteroplasmy and threshold effects shape mtDNA disease severity
Leigh syndrome: infant regression with symmetric basal ganglia/brainstem lesions
Elevated lactate (blood, CSF, MR spectroscopy) is a key clue
Rule out treatable mimics like SLC19A3 and CoQ10 deficiency

test.q: Which molecule do mitochondria mainly produce through oxidative phosphorylation?
test.explain: OXPHOS generates ATP. Lactate builds up when OXPHOS fails and cells shift to anaerobic metabolism.

test.q: From whom is mitochondrial DNA inherited?

A mix of normal and mutant mtDNA in a cell
Two copies of a nuclear gene being mutated

test.q: Why is lactate often elevated in mitochondrial disease?
test.explain: When OXPHOS fails, pyruvate is converted to lactate to keep glycolysis running.

test.explain: Complex I deficiency is the most common biochemical finding in Leigh syndrome.

test.explain: MELAS (m.3243A>G) features stroke-like episodes. A cherry-red spot belongs to lysosomal diseases.

test.explain: Infection and fever raise energy demand, pushing vulnerable regions past their threshold.

test.explain: Symptoms appear once the mutant fraction exceeds a tissue-specific threshold.

test.q: Human mtDNA is a circle of 16,569 base pairs encoding ___ genes.
test.explain: It has 37 genes: 13 OXPHOS subunits, 22 tRNAs and 2 rRNAs.

test.q: Leigh syndrome is also called subacute necrotizing ___.
test.explain: The name reflects necrotic lesions in the brain and spinal cord.

kidTest.q: What do mitochondria do?
kidTest.explain: Mitochondria are the cell's power plants.

kidTest.q: Why does the brain need a lot of energy?
choices: It stays busy day and night
It grows hair on the head
kidTest.explain: The brain is always busy, so it needs lots of energy.

kidTest.q: Who do you get mitochondrial genes from?
kidTest.explain: Mitochondrial genes come only from your mom.

kidTest.q: What does Leigh syndrome hurt?
kidTest.explain: It damages brain areas that control moving, breathing and swallowing.

kidTest.q: Mitochondria are tiny power p _ _ _ _ _ inside cells.
kidTest.explain: They make energy, just like power plants make electricity.

advancedTest.q: A mother with low m.8993T>G heteroplasmy has a child with Leigh syndrome at very high load. What best explains this?
choices: Tissue repair raising mutant load after the child's birth
A new nuclear mutation arising in the child alone
Paternal transmission of mutant mtDNA through sperm
The mitochondrial genetic bottleneck in the female germline
advancedTest.explain: The germline bottleneck allows large heteroplasmy shifts between generations through drift.

advancedTest.q: Chronic hypoxia rescuing Ndufs4 knockout mice suggests that neurodegeneration in Leigh syndrome is driven partly by:
advancedTest.explain: When the chain cannot use oxygen, tissue oxygen accumulates. Lowering it improved survival, implicating oxygen toxicity.

advancedTest.q: Why is urine preferred over blood for measuring m.3243A>G heteroplasmy in adults?
choices: Urine reflects paternal mtDNA more closely
Urine has no mtDNA, which avoids false results
Blood cells lack any mitochondrial DNA
advancedTest.explain: Mutant load falls in blood over time, so urine epithelium better reflects tissue burden.

advancedTest.q: Why were DdCBE base editors a breakthrough for mtDNA, when standard CRISPR was not?
choices: They replace whole mitochondria in cells
They work by cutting both DNA strands
They target nuclear OXPHOS genes instead
They avoid the need for guide RNA import
advancedTest.explain: Guide RNAs are not efficiently imported into mitochondria. Protein-only DdCBEs bypass this barrier.

lessons.title: Spinal Muscular Atrophy and SMN2 Copy Number

levels.kid:
Your spinal cord has special nerve cells called **motor neurons**. They carry messages from your brain to your muscles, like wires that tell a toy robot to move.

To stay healthy, motor neurons need a helper protein called **SMN**. Kids with **spinal muscular atrophy**, or SMA, have a broken main recipe for SMN. Without enough of it, the motor neurons get weak and the muscles get floppy.

Here is the clever part. Everyone has a backup recipe too, called SMN2. It is a bit smudged, so it makes only a little good protein. Having more copies of the backup usually means milder SMA.

Today, doctors have medicines that help the backup recipe work better, or that give the body a fixed recipe. Finding SMA early in babies helps most.
levels.hs:
**Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)** is a genetic disease in which the **lower motor neurons**, the nerve cells in the spinal cord that connect directly to muscles, slowly die. Muscles become weak and shrink (**atrophy**). The weakness affects the trunk and the muscles closest to the body most, and it can also weaken breathing and swallowing.

SMA is **autosomal recessive**. A child is affected when both copies of the **SMN1** gene are missing or broken. About 1 in 40 to 1 in 60 people is a silent carrier.

The SMN1 gene makes **survival motor neuron (SMN) protein**. Humans also have a nearly identical gene next to it called **SMN2**. One single-letter change in SMN2 makes the cell skip a section called **exon 7** in most of its messages. That produces a short, unstable protein. Only about 10% of SMN2 output is full-length and working.

The number of SMN2 copies varies from person to person, and it is the strongest predictor of how severe SMA will be.
- A baby with **type 1** SMA usually has 2 copies. Symptoms start before 6 months, and the baby never sits.
- People with **type 3** often have 3 to 4 copies. They learn to walk.

Today SMA is treatable. Many places now test newborns for it, so treatment can start before motor neurons are lost.
levels.college:
**Genetics.** About 95% of SMA cases are caused by **homozygous deletion of SMN1 exon 7** on chromosome 5q13. The deletion often results from gene conversion of SMN1 to SMN2. The remaining cases are compound heterozygotes, who carry one deletion plus a point mutation in the other copy. The 5q13 region contains an inverted duplication, which makes it prone to rearrangement and copy-number variation.

**The SMN1 vs SMN2 difference.** The two genes differ by a critical **C-to-T change at position 6 of exon 7 (c.840C>T)**. The change is silent at the protein level, but it alters splicing:
- It disrupts an **exonic splicing enhancer** that binds **SRSF1**.
- It creates a silencer site bound by **hnRNP A1**.
- As a result, most SMN2 transcripts skip exon 7, producing **SMNΔ7**, which is unstable and rapidly degraded.

**What SMN does.** SMN is ubiquitous. It forms the SMN complex with the Gemin proteins, which assembles **snRNPs** for the spliceosome. SMN also helps transport mRNA along axons. Why motor neurons are most vulnerable is still debated.

**Clinical types.**
- **Type 0**: prenatal onset.
- **Type 1** (Werdnig-Hoffmann): onset before 6 months; the child never sits.
- **Type 2**: the child sits but never walks.
- **Type 3** (Kugelberg-Welander): the child walks.
- **Type 4**: adult onset.

Typical features are proximal weakness, absent reflexes, and tongue fasciculations. Breathing relies on the diaphragm, which produces a bell-shaped chest and paradoxical breathing.

**Diagnosis.** MLPA or qPCR detects SMN1 deletion and counts SMN2 copies.

**Therapies.** Three approved therapies target the SMN pathway:
- **Nusinersen**: an intrathecal antisense oligonucleotide that blocks intronic splicing silencer N1 (ISS-N1) in intron 7, promoting inclusion of exon 7.
- **Risdiplam**: an oral small molecule that modifies SMN2 splicing.
- **Onasemnogene abeparvovec**: AAV9 gene replacement that delivers SMN1.
levels.phd:
**SMN2 as a disease modifier.** SMN2 copy number (typically 0 to 6 or more) inversely correlates with severity, but the relationship is not absolute. Some 2-copy patients are milder than expected. One explanation is the **c.859G>C** variant in SMN2 exon 7, which creates an enhancer and increases inclusion of exon 7. Other modifiers lie outside SMN entirely. **Plastin 3 (PLS3)** overexpression protected some SMN1-deleted women in discordant families (Oprea et al., 2008). Reduced **neurocalcin delta (NCALD)** is also protective. Both modifiers act by improving endocytosis at the neuromuscular junction.

**Splicing regulation.** The c.840C>T change shifts the balance between the SRSF1 enhancer and the hnRNP A1 silencer, and it engages Sam68. Krainer, Singh and colleagues mapped **ISS-N1**, a 15-nucleotide intronic silencer beginning at intron 7 position +10. ISS-N1 became the target of the 2'-O-methoxyethyl phosphorothioate antisense oligonucleotide **nusinersen**. Risdiplam and branaplam stabilize the interaction between U1 snRNP and the weak **5' splice site** of exon 7 and an exonic splicing enhancer, strengthening exon recognition.

**Mechanism of selective vulnerability.** Hypotheses fall into two camps:
- **The snRNP hypothesis.** SMN deficiency causes cell-wide defects in minor (U12) intron splicing. Affected targets include Stasimon (TMEM41B), which has been implicated in Drosophila and zebrafish sensory-motor circuits.
- **Local axonal roles.** SMN deficiency impairs transport of β-actin mRNA and other cargo along axons.

Mouse work suggests that SMA is a circuit disease. Proprioceptive synapses onto motor neurons are lost early, and p53 activation through aberrant splicing of Mdm2 and Mdm4 drives motor neuron death. Peripheral tissues, including the liver, heart and pancreas, are also affected in severe models.

**Timing.** In type 1 SMA, motor unit number estimates collapse within the first months after birth. Restoring SMN in Δ7 mice works only within an early window, which explains why presymptomatic treatment works best.

**Landmark trials.** ENDEAR (nusinersen) showed improved event-free survival in infantile-onset SMA. START (onasemnogene) showed survival without permanent ventilation in all 15 infants. The NURTURE study showed that presymptomatic treatment allowed most 2-copy infants to sit and walk.
levels.expert:
**Newborn screening.** SMA was added to the US Recommended Uniform Screening Panel in 2018. Screening uses real-time PCR on dried blood spots to detect the absence of SMN1 exon 7. Important pitfalls:
- Screening misses the roughly 5% of patients who are compound heterozygotes with a point mutation.
- It does not identify carriers.
- SMN2 copy counts can be misread, for example because of SMN1/SMN2 hybrid genes, or because standard assays cannot distinguish 4 copies from 5 or more.
- Positive screens need confirmation.

Consensus guidance (the Glascock working group, updated 2020) recommends immediate treatment for infants with 2 or 3 SMN2 copies. Most groups now also treat 4-copy infants rather than watching and waiting. Before AAV9 therapy, clinicians check **anti-AAV9 antibodies**.

**Choosing among therapies.** The three therapies have different practical concerns:
- **Onasemnogene**: the risks are hepatotoxicity, thrombotic microangiopathy, and thrombocytopenia. Corticosteroid prophylaxis is used, and risk rises with age and weight.
- **Nusinersen**: the burdens are repeated lumbar punctures, which become difficult after spinal fusion surgery for scoliosis, and monitoring for thrombocytopenia and renal toxicity.
- **Risdiplam**: it is systemic. Off-target splicing effects and teratogenicity in animal studies require attention to contraception.

Combination or add-on use is common in practice, but evidence comes mainly from RESPOND and from registries.

**The new phenotype.** Treated children survive with a new natural history. Many have residual weakness, scoliosis, hip problems, bulbar dysfunction, and, in severe 2-copy cases, distal involvement, cognitive concerns, and possibly late motor neuron decline. Whether gene therapy remains durable for years is an open question, since AAV episomes are lost if cells divide, although motor neurons are postmitotic. Biomarkers include **neurofilament light chain** in CSF and plasma, which falls rapidly with treatment, and CMAP amplitude.

**Beyond SMN.** Muscle-directed add-ons that target myostatin, such as apitegromab and taldefgrobep, are being tested to boost strength. **Intrathecal onasemnogene (OAV101 IT)** is being studied for older and heavier patients.

**Mimics.** Non-5q SMAs include SMARD1, caused by IGHMBP2 mutations, which presents with diaphragmatic palsy, distal weakness, and early respiratory failure. They are not detected by screening and need a separate workup. SMA is also a model for neurosurgeons and spine teams: intrathecal access after spinal fusion may need laminotomy windows or image-guided transforaminal approaches.

keyPoints: SMA is autosomal recessive loss of lower motor neurons due to missing SMN1
SMN2 differs by a C-to-T change that makes most transcripts skip exon 7
Only about 10% of SMN2 output is full-length SMN protein
More SMN2 copies generally means milder SMA (types 0 to 4)
Nusinersen and risdiplam fix SMN2 splicing; onasemnogene replaces SMN1
Newborn screening enables presymptomatic treatment, which works best

test.q: Which cells degenerate in spinal muscular atrophy?
choices: Sensory neurons in dorsal root ganglia
Upper motor neurons in the cortex
Lower motor neurons in the spinal cord
test.explain: SMA destroys anterior horn (lower) motor neurons. Upper motor neurons are spared, which is why reflexes are lost rather than increased.

test.q: What is the inheritance pattern of 5q SMA?
test.explain: Both copies of SMN1 must be missing or broken. Carriers are common, roughly 1 in 40 to 60 people.

test.q: What happens to most SMN2 transcripts?
choices: Exon 1 is duplicated in the message
Exon 7 gains a premature start codon
Transcription of the gene is blocked
test.explain: The c.840C>T change shifts splicing so that most SMN2 messages lack exon 7, producing unstable SMNΔ7 protein.

test.q: Which factor best predicts SMA severity?
choices: The size of the SMN1 deletion
Which parent passed on the deletion
test.explain: Each SMN2 copy adds some full-length protein, so more copies usually means a milder type.

test.q: A child sits independently but has never walked. Which SMA type fits?
test.explain: Type 2 patients sit but never walk. Type 1 children never sit, and type 3 patients walk.

test.q: How does nusinersen work?
choices: It blocks myostatin in skeletal muscle
It degrades the SMNΔ7 protein faster
It delivers a new SMN1 gene in a virus
It blocks a splicing silencer in SMN2 intron 7
test.explain: This antisense oligonucleotide binds ISS-N1 so that exon 7 is included. Gene delivery is how onasemnogene works, not nusinersen.

test.q: Onasemnogene abeparvovec uses which vector?
test.explain: AAV9 crosses into motor neurons and delivers a functional SMN1 copy.

test.q: What is a core function of SMN protein?
choices: Pumping sodium out of motor neurons
Forming the myelin sheath around axons
test.explain: With the Gemin proteins, SMN assembles snRNPs. It also helps transport mRNA along axons.

test.q: Why does newborn screening matter so much in SMA?
choices: It identifies which parent carries the deletion
Therapy works best before motor neurons are lost
It helps prevent carriers from passing the gene
It replaces the need for any confirmatory test
test.explain: Motor neurons are lost quickly in early infancy. The NURTURE study showed that presymptomatic treatment gave the best outcomes.

test.q: Which gene, when missing on both chromosomes, causes most SMA?
test.explain: About 95% of patients have homozygous deletion of SMN1 exon 7.

test.q: Most SMN2 transcripts lack exon ___, giving an unstable protein.
test.explain: Skipping exon 7 produces SMNΔ7, which is rapidly degraded.

test.q: What is the oral small molecule that modifies SMN2 splicing?
test.explain: Risdiplam is taken by mouth and increases inclusion of exon 7.

kidTest.q: What do motor neurons do?
kidTest.explain: They carry the move signal from the brain to the muscles.

kidTest.q: In SMA, what happens to the muscles?
kidTest.explain: Without healthy motor neurons, muscles get weak.

kidTest.q: What is the backup recipe called?
kidTest.explain: SMN2 is the backup. It makes only a little good protein.

kidTest.q: More copies of the backup usually means:
kidTest.explain: More backup copies make more good protein.

kidTest.q: SMN is a helper p _ _ _ _ _ _ that motor neurons need.
kidTest.explain: SMN protein keeps motor neurons healthy.

advancedTest.q: A patient has 2 SMN2 copies but an unexpectedly mild course. Which finding best explains this?
choices: A second SMN1 deletion on the other chromosome
A c.859G>C variant that enhances inclusion of exon 7 in SMN2
Heterozygous loss of one SMN2 copy
Reduced expression of plastin 3 in motor neurons
advancedTest.explain: c.859G>C creates an enhancer that increases full-length SMN2 output. Reduced plastin 3 would not protect; it is PLS3 overexpression that is protective.

advancedTest.q: Newborn screening is negative, but an infant develops classic SMA weakness. What is the most likely genetic explanation?
choices: Homozygous deletion of SMN1 exon 7 on both alleles
A large deletion in the mitochondrial DNA
Having five or more SMN2 copies in the genome
One deletion plus an SMN1 point mutation
advancedTest.explain: The PCR screen detects the absence of SMN1 exon 7. One deleted allele plus a point mutation leaves exon 7 present, so the screen misses it.

advancedTest.q: Why would nusinersen alone be predicted to fail in a patient with zero SMN2 copies?
choices: Its target sequence lies in SMN2 pre-mRNA
It needs AAV9 antibodies in order to work
It is unable to leave the cerebrospinal fluid
It targets the SMN1 promoter region instead
advancedTest.explain: Nusinersen corrects SMN2 splicing at ISS-N1. With no SMN2 there is nothing to correct, so gene replacement would be required.

advancedTest.q: Which observation best supports a time-limited therapeutic window in SMA?
choices: AAV episomes are rapidly lost from motor neurons
SMN restoration in Δ7 mice rescues mainly when given early
SMN2 copy number climbs as children grow older
Plasma neurofilament light chain rises after treatment begins
advancedTest.explain: Late SMN restoration fails once motor neurons are lost, matching the early collapse of motor units in humans. Neurofilament light actually falls with treatment.
